big_idea: Pattern-makers plan a core, repeat it, extend it, and explain it.
learning_intention: We are learning to plan, build, lead, and explain a parade pattern that we made ourselves.
student_learning_goal: I can plan a parade pattern, lead it, and explain the core to a friend.
success_criteria: I can plan a parade with a core that repeats.
I can build my parade and extend it forward and backward.
I can show my core a second way using sounds or my body.
I can explain my core to my partner.
lesson_specific_materials: Anchor chart from previous four lessons (PATTERN, CORE, MISSING, EXTEND visible)
Junior Pattern Conductor certificates (provided in assessment_suite stage; one per student)
Summative rubric — one copy on a clipboard per teacher (provided in assessment_suite stage)
Optional: small handheld bell or shaker for the closing celebration

minds_on.hook: Today is the big day. You have everything you need in your toolbox — and YOU are the conductor.
minds_on.teacher_script:
Bring children to the carpet. Stand by the anchor chart, which now has all four words: PATTERN, CORE, MISSING, EXTEND. Hold up Coco.

Say to students: 'Friends, look at our chart. We have learned so much. Day 1 we learned what a PATTERN is. Day 2 we found the CORE. Day 3 we showed the same core in three different ways. Day 4 we fixed parades that were MISSING animals, and we learned to EXTEND them — forward AND backward.' Tap each word as you say it.

'Today is your big day. Today YOU are the Pattern Conductor. You will plan a parade. You will build it. You will show it a second way. And you will lead a friend through it. Coco is going to be watching very carefully — and so am I — because today everyone gets to earn the Junior Pattern Conductor certificate.'

Quick whole-class warm-up: clap-stomp three times. 'Ready, conductors? Let's begin.'
student_actions: Sit on the carpet and review the four anchor-chart words as a class.
Repeat the four words aloud as the teacher taps each.
Move to their desk or workspace when dismissed.

steps.instruction: Phase 1 — Plan (5 min). Each child receives the 'Lead Your Own Parade' worksheet (page 1). They draw or sticker their chosen core in the 'My Core' box and place a loop around it. They may pick AB, ABB, ABC, or ABBA — their choice.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'First job: plan your CORE. Pick how many things will be in your core. Draw it in the My Core box. Then circle it with the loop — that shows you know what repeats.'

steps.instruction: Phase 2 — Build (10 min). Children build their parade on the worksheet's parade strip, extending the core forward AND backward to fill 8 cells. Teacher circulates with the summative rubric clipboard and begins one-on-one conferences during this phase.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Now build your parade. The middle four animals are easy — they come right from your core, repeating it. The hard part is the two on each end. Make sure they keep the pattern going BOTH ways. I will come around and ask each of you to read your parade to me.'

steps.instruction: Phase 3 — Translate (5 min). Children fill the second strip on their worksheet with the SAME core, but using sounds OR body icons (their choice). They can reference the M3 cards if needed. Teacher continues conferences.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Last building job: show your same core a second way. Sounds, like clap-stomp. Or bodies, like tall-small. Same core — just a different way of showing it.'

steps.instruction: Phase 4 — Lead (5 min). Children move to the carpet in pairs. Each child leads their partner through their parade: reads the animal version aloud, points to and explains the core, walks the partner through the second version, and finally asks the partner 'What would come after my last animal? What would come before my first animal?' Then they swap.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Final job. Find a partner. Take turns being the conductor. When it's your turn: read your parade out loud, show your partner your core, lead them through your second version, and ask them what comes next AND what came before. Then it's your partner's turn.'

steps.instruction: Phase 5 — REVISE & REFLECT (8 min). Children return to their desk with their worksheet. The teacher prompts: 'Look at your parade now that you've led your partner. Did anything feel wrong? Did your partner stop you anywhere? Find ONE thing on your worksheet to fix — the missing element on the end, the second representation that didn't quite match the core, or the loop placement.' Each child must mark or change at least one element (REFINE). Then they draw a small star next to the part they're proudest of and a small question mark next to the part that was hardest (REFLECT). The teacher walks the room with the summative rubric clipboard, looking for whether children can self-identify an error and address it without prompting.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Two final jobs, Pattern Conductors. First — you just heard your parade out loud and led a friend. Be your own teacher now. Find ONE thing on your worksheet to revise. Pick up your pencil and fix it. Pattern Conductors always check their own work. Then — draw a star next to the part you're PROUDEST of and a question mark next to the part that was HARDEST. We'll share these in our circle.'

differentiation.for_emerging: AB cores only. Pre-print the parade strip with the first cell of the core already filled to give a launchpad. Allow the child to lead a single partner with the teacher beside them, scaffolding the four-step lead routine.
differentiation.for_extending: Encourage ABBA, AABB, or ABC cores. After their partner-lead, invite them to lead a small group of 3–4 children through their parade. Ask them to explain WHY their second version has the same core.
differentiation.for_ell_or_iep: Allow the child to lead by walking the parade physically rather than explaining verbally. Accept gestures and pointing as evidence. The teacher conference can be visual: 'Show me your core. Show me what comes next. Show me your second way.'
differentiation.for_movement_learners: These children typically excel at the Lead phase. Encourage them to invent a body-movement version and lead the partner physically through it — turning the worksheet into performance.

formative_check.what_to_look_for: This is the summative — record evidence per expectation. A7.1: did the child create a valid pattern? A7.2: can they identify and explain the core? A7.3: did they produce a second representation with the same core? A7.4: did they extend in both directions and answer 'what comes before' and 'what comes after' correctly?
formative_check.how_to_record: Use the summative rubric (one row per child, one column per expectation, score 1–4). Record evidence-based anecdotal notes for any score below 3 or any standout score of 4.

discussion_prompts: What was your favourite part of being the Pattern Conductor today?
Who would you like to thank for helping you learn about patterns this week?
consolidation.exit_routine: Gather on the carpet. Each child receives a Junior Pattern Conductor certificate (printed from the assessment_suite stage). The teacher reads each child's name aloud, says one specific thing they observed during the summative ('I saw _____ extend a parade backward all by themselves'), and hands them the certificate. Class applauds after each. Optional: ring a small bell or shaker after each name.

assessment_in_this_lesson.evidence_collected: Completed 'Lead Your Own Parade' worksheet (Phases 1–3 visible artifact), one-on-one teacher conference notes captured during Phase 2/3, and partner-lead observation from Phase 4. Each child receives a 1–4 score on the summative rubric for each of A7.1, A7.2, A7.3, A7.4.
assessment_in_this_lesson.rationale: This is the unit's summative. The four-phase structure (Plan-Build-Translate-Lead) is deliberately designed so that each phase generates evidence for at least one expectation. Plan/Build covers A7.1 and A7.2; Translate covers A7.3; Lead covers A7.4 (and re-anchors A7.2). The teacher can score most children during conferences in Phase 2/3 and confirm during the Lead phase.

expanded_walkthrough.title: Phase 5 — when self-revision becomes the assessment evidence
expanded_walkthrough.rationale: Phase 5 is the keystone of the summative. The four earlier phases produce student work; Phase 5 produces evidence of metacognition — whether the child can step back, see their own pattern through fresh eyes, and identify what needs fixing. For K, the move from 'finished my work' to 'check my work' is a real cognitive lift. The teacher's job during Phase 5 is to NOT point out errors — instead, prompt the child to find them. The script below covers the most common stuck points.
expanded_walkthrough.setup: Each child has their completed Lead-Your-Own-Parade worksheet in front of them. Pencil and a few backup animal stickers are at hand. The summative rubric clipboard is with the teacher. The Core Loop M5 is at the carpet for any child who needs to re-anchor. Carpet still shows the partner-leading partners from Phase 4.
expanded_walkthrough.teacher_script:
Walk to the first child. Crouch down. 'When your partner walked through your parade, did anything sound off?' Wait six seconds. If the child says 'no,' don't accept it. Slide your finger along their core. 'Tell me your core out loud. Bea, Bibi, Bea, Bibi. Now read me your parade strip out loud, cell by cell.' Children almost always spot a mismatch when they SAY it aloud — a Bibi where there should be a Bea, or a missing animal at the end. The moment of recognition is your formative gate.

Move to a child who has confidently extended forward but not backward. 'Tell me what comes BEFORE your first Bea.' Often the child stops. 'Could you fix the very first cell to show what would come before?' Watch whether they apply the core inverted. If they do — note it on the rubric as 'extends backward.' If they don't — leave the worksheet alone and let it stand as evidence at L2 on A7.4.

If a child confidently says 'nothing's wrong,' bring out the partner version. 'Take your second-version strip — the one with sounds or bodies. Read it again. Does each cell of the SOUND version match the same cell of the ANIMAL version?' Mismatch in translation is one of the most common errors AND one of the most diagnostic — child knows the rule for animals but loses it when translating to a second representation.

If a child has nothing to revise on either strip and the partner work was clean, stretch them. 'If your parade marched all the way to twenty animals — what would the twentieth one be?' Have them write the answer in the corner. That's your A7.x Level 4 evidence.
expected_student_responses: (Refines fluently) Spots a missing element at the end, fills it confidently. Notes 'I forgot the last Bea.' Records on rubric as L3 on A7.1.
(Refines with prompt) After reading aloud, says 'oh — that one should have been Finn.' Erases and corrects.
(Cannot self-spot) Says 'looks fine to me.' Even after reading aloud, doesn't catch the error. Note on rubric as L1-L2 on A7.4.
(Stretches) Confidently extends the parade in writing to twenty cells with no help. Note as L4 evidence.
common_misconceptions: 'My work is finished' = 'my work is correct.' (Child equates completion with correctness; the entire concept of self-checking is new.)

Translation across representations is symbolic, not literal. (Child writes a sound-version that has the right number of items but a different rule than their animal version — they've forgotten the core has to stay constant.)
Extending backward is impossible from a partial strip. (Child can extend forward but freezes when asked what would come before cell 1, even after the L4 walkthrough.)
recovery_moves: Make them read aloud. 'Tell me your core, then read me your parade cell by cell.' Saying it audibly reveals 80% of errors without the teacher pointing at anything.
Cross-check the two representations. Ask the child to read cell-1 of strip-A then cell-1 of strip-B, then cell-2 of A then cell-2 of B. The mismatch becomes physically apparent.
Loop the core on each strip. Use M5 visibly to anchor what the core IS, then ask 'do these two strips really have the same core?' The visual move bypasses the verbal confusion.

worksheet_brief.purpose: Summative performance task artifact — Phases 1–3 (Plan, Build, Translate) generate the visible evidence for the rubric. Phase 4 (Lead) is observational and is captured on the rubric, not the worksheet.

parts_outline.task: Plan the core. Empty box at the top of the page labelled 'My Core'. Student draws or stickers their chosen core (2-, 3-, or 4-element). A small loop frame icon prompts them to mark the repeating part with a circle.

Build the parade. A long parade strip with 8 cells: 4 in the middle that the student fills using their core, and 2 cells extending past each end that the student must also fill (extending forward and backward).

Show it another way. A second parade strip below Part 2. Student translates the SAME core into a sound version OR a body version (their choice), drawing or stickering icons. A small caption box reads: 'My core was the same. I just used ___ instead of animals.'

expected_image_assets: All four animal thumbnails (Bea, Finn, Bibi, Moss)
Sound icons (clap, stomp, hum, tap) matching M3
Loop frame icon (small, in the corner of Part 1's My Core box)
Parade strip layout for Part 2 with cells extending past both ends
Coco the Conductor in the worksheet header, holding a small certificate to signal this is the summative
